To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
certain mutant forms of p53 confer a dominant, gain of function phenotype that disrupts the mitotic spindle checkpoint and generates polyploidy in mammalian cells.
p53(RSC) mutations confer a dominant, gain of function phenotype in which the spindle checkpoint fails, leading to polyploidization of the cell.
a subset of p53 mutations confers a dominant gain-of-function activity in spindle checkpoint control.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of p53 in the control of the spindle checkpoint, which normally ensures the accurate segregation of chromosomes.
the mechanisms by which p53 mutations can lead to genomic instability and cancer.
the role of p53 in the regulation of cell cycle checkpoints, particularly those that monitor the status of the mitotic spindle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
p53 mutations can cause cancer by two mechanisms, loss of tumor suppressor function, and by gain-of-function.
the p53(RSC) mutation confers a gain-of-function phenotype on the spindle checkpoint that is dominant over the normal checkpoint.
p53(RSC) is an example of a gain of function p53 mutant that confers a phenotype of genomic instability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a common class of dominant, mutant p53 allele generates genomic instability.
p53 mutations can be oncogenic by a mechanism that is independent of p53 tumor suppression.
p53(RSC) mutant allele can cause cancer by both loss-of-function (tumor suppressor activity) and gain-of-function (genomic instability).
The main takeaway from our work is that
a dominant, gain of function activity of p53 can lead to genomic instability.
p53 mutations can promote cancer not only by loss of function but also by gain-of-function.
p53 mutations can have both dominant, gain-of function activities that promote cancer progression and loss-of-function activities that contribute to cancer development.
